newsitem.title: USA: N. Carolina court upholds school funding formula.
newsitem.headline: N. Carolina court upholds school funding formula.

text.p: The North Carolina Supreme Court upheld the state's school funding formula, ruling that students were entitled to "a sound basic education" but not an equal one.
In its 6-1 ruling Thursday, the court acknowledged that per pupil spending in poor districts might not equal that in wealthy districts. But the court said that did not violate the state constitution.

"The North Carolina Constitution requires that all childen have the opportunity for a sound basic education, but it does not require that equal educational opportunities be afforded students in all of the school districts of the state," the state," Chief Justice Burley Mitchell wrote in the ruling.

North Carolina spends more than 40 percent of its general fund budget on public primary and secondary schools, but requires local governments to bear capital expenses plus 25 percent of operating expenses.

Students, parents, guardians and school boards in five poor counties sued the state and the North Carolina Board of Education, claiming children in those districts were denied their constitutional right to equal educational opportunities.

Eleven large, wealthier counties joined the lawsuit, claiming that the funding formula did not adequately address the special needs of large urban districts with a greater share of students who need special education or do not speak English.

The court said there was no constitutional right to equal funding and dismissed that portion of the lawsuit. But it said a lower court should hear the plaintiffs' claims that the some poor districts did not provide an adequate education. That portion of the case was sent back to Wake County Superior Court for trial.

The court defined "a sound basic education" as one that provides students with enough knowledge of English, math, physical sciences, geography, history, economics and politics "to function in a rapidly changing society."

It said students should also be provided with enough academic and vocational skills to pursue a secondary education or find gainful employment and "make informed choces on issues that affect the comunity, state and nation."
